did_you_know.text: Did you know? Job describes his spirit as broken and his days as passing away, summing up his deep distress with the words, “The graves are my home”—as though death is already near.
Did you know? Job says that mockers are the only people around him, and that his eye grows weak from continually facing their words.
Did you know? Job asks God to guarantee his safety—to commit, as it were, to protecting him—because he can find no one else to support him.
Did you know? Job claims that God has hidden understanding from his friends, so they are unable to encourage and comfort him properly.
Did you know? Job describes himself as having become a proverb and a laughingstock among the nations—in other words, a symbol of someone whose suffering has become an example on other people’s lips.
Did you know? Job connects his anger and suffering with the weakening of his eyesight, and describes his body as a shadow—a picture emphasizing his physical decline.

Did you know? Despite his difficult condition, Job describes the response of the upright and the innocent: they are appalled by injustice, and the innocent rise up against the hypocrite and flatterer.
Did you know? Amid his description of suffering, Job speaks of the strength of the righteous: they hold firmly to their way, and those whose hands remain pure grow ever more courageous.
Did you know? Job invites his friends to speak again, but sarcastically declares that he will find no wise person among them—a direct criticism of their advice and speeches.
Did you know? Job describes Sheol as his home and darkness as the place where he makes his bed, expressing deep despair about life and his sense that death is near.

Did you know? At the end of the chapter, Job describes his hope and himself descending together to Sheol and resting in the dust, bringing the chapter to a close without any clear solution or comfort.
